description: Model validation techniques are critically important in data science work. Here, Nate Silver tests the empirical distribution of US election polling against what we would expect based on  the expected numerical distribution. #กรีนสกรีน  #datascience #datascientist #dataanalytics #2024elections #datasciencetok #statistics
hashtags: กรีนสกรีน, datascience, datascientist, dataanalytics, 2024elections, datasciencetok, statistics
_transcript: Nate Silver just came out with a pretty bombshell report suggesting that is almost guaranteed that the U.S. polling data is incorrect. In fact, he argues the probability that the U.S. election polling data is correct is less than 1 in 9 trillion. Now, he is using a data model validation technique that if you're a data scientist and you're running some fairly complicated models with weightings and different covariates and structures, this is really good practice. Now, there have been thousands of U.S. election polls in the United States, and they tend to have a margin of error of around like plus or minus 3 or 4 percentage points. But because this is essentially a one-to-one matchup, being plus or minus 3 points means that it should be a 6 percentage point gap between the two candidates. Right, so if they're actually tied, but you get a plus 3 errors per se like Kamala Harris, that takes away 3 from Donald Trump, and so the gap should be about 6. So when you think about a polling's margin of error or a confidence interval when you're doing a statistical model is that under repeated sampling, so if you repeat this experiment or if you repeat these polls and these surveys like over and over again, you should get a distribution of results that covers the span of this margin of error. So if the race was tied, you should get polls that are effectively normally distributed around a zero gap, but where there are outliers of plus 3, minus 3. And what Nate showed was if given the sample sizes of these polls, we should have seen no more than 55% of the polls being within 2.5 percentage points if the race was actually tied. So if the race was tied, we would expect to see the maximum number of close polls, right? So we don't even have to worry about the fact of the cases where they're not tied. But if the case was tied, we should see no more than 55% of the polls being within 2.5%. But in reality, we're seeing more than 80% of the polls that are being within plus or minus 2.5 percentage points. And given the number of polls and the sample size of these polls, Nate estimates the probability of this happening by random chance alone would be only 1 in 9.5 trillion. So the problem here is that it's really easy to lie with statistics, and this comes up with data scientists all the time when we're dealing with our stakeholders that basically want to hear the results that they want to hear. So these pollsters are going out and they're surveying people, but then they apply weights, and the weights are determined via a likely voter model that they have complete control over. So if they get a result that should be a normal outlier in random sampling that says, you know, Harris is up plus 4 or Trump is up plus 4, they will put their finger on the scale and they'll adjust these likely voter models so that it comes out closer to plus 1, minus 1 in either direction. And so what we're seeing here is that the empirical distribution of polling results is not what we would expect based on characteristics of the normal distribution and of the surveys and the sample sizes, and that is a huge red flag that there is a problem with the polling.

description: With the midterm elections now less than a year away, a new PBS News/NPR/Marist poll has signs of hope for Democrats and a few red flags for Republicans. Amna Nawaz and NPR's Domenico Montanaro break down the numbers and discuss what's resonating with voters. #pbsnewshour #newshour #pbsnews #politics #midterms #elections #npr #marist #democrat #republican

_transcript: With the midterm elections now less than a year away, a new PBS News-NPR-Marist poll has signs of hope for Democrats and a few red flags for Republicans. So what is resonating with voters? NPR senior political editor and correspondent Domenico Montanaro is here to break down the numbers. Good to see you. Hey, good to see you. Let's jump in. So Democrats came off some big election wins in New Jersey and New York City and Virginia a couple of weeks ago. Seems like they have an advantage. Midterms are still a long way off. But what does the poll show? And in a lot of places across the country, up and down the ballot, really. And I think that what this poll shows is that Democrats have a huge advantage right now. And the real issue is because of affordability. But what the poll shows is by 55 to 41 margin, Democrats, people say that they would pick a Democrat in their district if the midterm elections were held today. Now, why is that important? It's a plus 14 advantage on what's known as the congressional ballot. When you have that large of a lead, it is really indicative of a potential wave. I mean, if you look back to 2022, for example, Democrats had only between an average of zero to four points. They lost nine seats in 2018. Democrats had an advantage between six and 12 points in our poll, and they obviously won big 40 seat advantage. Now, most people don't expect that we're going to see a wave of that kind next year. But right now starts out with Democrats with a big advantage. And a big piece of that is because of independents and how they've slid away. I mean, a 61 to 28 percent margin, independents say that they would pick a Democrat. These are major red flags and warning signs for the Republican Party right now. And we know a lot can happen in the next year. But that also includes whatever happens on this redistricting front. We've seen efforts by President Trump and the Republicans, counter efforts by the Democrats in California. This is all tied up in the courts right now. But does any of this make the Democratic polling advantage moot? You know, it depends on how this winds up shaking out. But frankly, we're seeing some evidence in the past week or so that this could boomerang on Republicans potentially. You know, Trump wanted to get five seats out of Texas. A court this week said that Texas's maps got to go back to the drawing board. Now, eventually they might get what they want, but they're also banking a lot on Latinos in South Texas having moved toward Donald Trump. And what we're seeing in our polling in the elections is that Latinos have really slid away from Donald Trump and Republicans. They moved over because of affordability. And what we're hearing from a lot of those voters is that they don't feel that Trump has done enough to address lowering costs and that they are upset with how he's approached deportations in this country, feeling like, you know, they were OK with supporting criminals, but not OK with deporting people in their communities in the same way that they see it being conducted. And like we've talked about, prices are the real issue, right? I mean, when you look at the issues inside our poll, 57 percent say that lowering prices should be the administration's top priority. Nothing else comes close. You can see there immigration, 16 percent in second. And even a plurality of Republicans there say that lowering prices should be Trump's top priority. Meanwhile, if you look at the Republican Party, we have seen some rifts. We've been covering Marjorie Taylor Greene's break with the president, him calling her a traitor. But how are Americans looking at the president's performance right now? Yeah, I think that this is a huge reason why maybe there's an opening for other Republicans to show some independence. I think they're going to be watching what happens with Marjorie Taylor Greene to see if she suffers any political consequences, as Trump says that she will. If she doesn't, I wonder what that's going to mean as Trump continues to look further and further like a lame duck and is on the wrong side of these issues. In the polling here, only 39 percent say that they approve of the job that Trump is doing. And when you look inside the numbers, only 24 percent of independents approve of the job he's doing. Now, the other number, as you see, nine in 10 Republicans still sticking with the president. So it continues to put Republican candidates in a vice, because we're seeing that when Trump is not on the ballot, Republican MAGA base voters don't necessarily show up. We heard from a lot of Republican voters in this poll who said that they are pro-Trump, but they're not necessarily voting for Republican candidates. That is a real problem for them, because they need to be able to show some independence from Trump to be able to say, to appeal to those crossover voters and to independents. But they can't alienate the base. Can I ask you quickly about one more thing we saw in here? Some bigger frustrations among American voters with political institutions and beyond. What do you take away from that? People don't like anything. If you look at what they think about the confidence in institutions, really bad numbers here for almost everybody, including us in the media, by the way, only 25 percent approve of what we're doing. Full results, of course, always available online. Domenico Montanaro, NPR, always good to see you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you.

_transcript: President Trump's hardline immigration policies have earned mixed reviews from Americans. That's according to our latest PBS News NPR Marist poll released today. To walk us through some of the new numbers, I'm joined now by NPR's Domenico Montanaro. Great to see you. Hey, great to be with you. Let's pick up on immigration that Laura was just reporting on. It was a central issue for Mr. Trump's re-election campaign. How do voters look at this issue at this point in his presidency? Well, his handling of immigration mirrors his overall job approval rating. Only 43% say that they approve of the job that the president is doing when it comes to handling immigration. 52% disapprove. And like I said, that's the same number as approve and disapprove of him overall. He doesn't get really good marks on almost anything either. Only 41% approve of his job on foreign policy and just 39% on the economy. So immigration's the best of those, but still not great. Domenico, like a lot of issues, it gets more interesting the deeper you go. Our colleague Josh Barajas spoke to a number of voters about the president's immigration agenda. One, a man named Stephen Singh, who's an independent voter in California, had this to say. I would love a more streamlined pathway to citizenship for immigrants. I don't wanna see students deported. I hate to see students being deported as a weapon to spread someone's political ideals and to silence others. So the nuanced answer is there are some cases where I think his immigration policy is spot on and there's some where I think it's overstepping the bounds. Is that view showing up in the polling? Yeah, I mean, in reality, views of immigration are much more nuanced than sometimes the political debate lends itself to be. Republicans feel very strongly one way, Democrats feel very strongly another way. When we look directly at deportation policies and whether or not they're making the country more safe, less safe, or not having any impact, you can see they're 43% say that Trump's deportation policies are making the country safer, 33% say less safe, a quarter say no impact at all. When it comes to how that breaks down by party, as we were talking about, 81% of Republicans think that his policies are making the country safer. Only 17% of Democrats are with just 34% of independents as well saying that they think that his policies are making the country safer. And when it comes to who is being impacted and targeted in these policies, how do Americans view that? And reflecting a lot of what we heard that voter say there, there's a real range. There's a wide range here. When it comes to violent offenders, people who are convicted of crimes who are in the country without permanent legal status, 80% say deport them. When it comes to nonviolent offenders, those convicted of crimes but nonviolent crimes, almost 6 in 10 also say to deport them as well. But it gets a lot trickier for Trump the further down we go. We heard that person talk about those who have overstayed visas. Only 49% say that they should be deported, real split in the country. And when it comes to those industry workers, people in the food and agricultural industry, for example, 44% say that they should be deported. A majority say don't do that. So we've seen a number of these immigration policies, other policies of the president, ending up in court. There's a mixed bag in terms of where the rulings are landed. But there are questions being raised by the president and his supporters about whether or not the president needs to comply with those court orders. How do people feel about this issue? Well, overall, I mean, 82% of people said that they think that any president should follow court orders, even if he or she doesn't like them. When you dig a little bit deeper into those numbers, though, 22% of Republicans only said that they feel strongly about this, as opposed to big majorities of independents and Democrats who said strongly that they think a president should follow this. So I guess if there's something they really don't like, they might be able to give Trump a little bit of leash. Here's the other thing that stuck out to me. Going into Independence Day, the poll showed a striking number of people who say they are concerned about the state of democracy in America. What should we understand about that? Yeah, it's really interesting. 3 quarters of people say that there is a serious threat to democracy. 3 quarters of people also say that politically motivated violence is a major threat, a major problem in the country as well. So you have a lot of people who really feel uneasy right now about the situation in the country, the polarization that exists in the country. But they have very little faith in their political leadership as well. Fascinating look where the country is right now. NPR's Domenico Montanaro. Thank you so much. You're welcome.

_transcript: If the polls are correct, this is going to be an extremely close election, and we might not know who won on election night. And that gap between the polls closing and waiting for a winner can spark tons of misinformation or confusing data as you watch the results come in. So here's a few questions and answers about what to look for on election night. Why are results taking longer than election night? There are a couple reasons why we might not know who won the presidential race on election night. It could come down to voting behaviors, how close the election is in some states, and it could also just come down to the simple process of counting and processing mail ballots. Now in the 2020 election, voters across the country in the pandemic shifted to mail voting as a safe way to cast their ballot. That voting method has continued to be of wide preference this election, but in different states there's different laws governing how they can be counted. In Pennsylvania and in Wisconsin, two very important swing states, election officials cannot start processing ballots until the morning of election day, and that can lead to a backup in ballots that need to be counted and tabulated. When news organizations look to make their call on election night in a really close race, that can come down to the final ballots. The second question is, what happens if I think I saw a vote total go down? We want to point out that this is an extremely rare occurrence, but there are times where mistakes can be made. They're often caught within minutes. The New York Times gets its election night results from the Associated Press, which combines data from state and county election offices with the work of thousands of correspondents across the country. The AP then checks those vote totals for any kind of inconsistencies. The Times also does its own verification process to look for any other inconsistencies or problems in the posted results. It's a meticulous process going through reporting results, but in the social media age, a simple screenshot of one of those errors can create a disinformation landscape and erode trust in the final results of an election. The last question is, why did one candidate appear to be ahead and then a lot of votes come in at the last second for the other candidate? We can go back to Pennsylvania in 2020 to see what happened there. They were inundated with mail ballots. That took a long time to count, and so on election night, most of the mail ballots from Democratic areas like Philadelphia and Pittsburgh had not yet been counted, so it looked like former President Trump was winning Pennsylvania. But as those ballots were counted over the next four days from Democratic areas, President Biden eventually caught up and the race was called for him. This delayed reporting results can sometimes lead to what are known as mirages, which is when it appears that a certain candidate is leading simply because more of their area's ballots have been counted and reported than the other candidates. The timing of results can sometimes simply come down to where votes were cast. In some states, rural areas are faster at uploading their results than urban areas. In some states, they report mail ballots instantly. In others, it could take well into the night or even in the coming days. And in some states, early in-person voting is all reported at once. So while it might be frustrating to not be able to know who won the presidential election or who controls Congress within hours of polls closing, this is just the system working as it should. _transcript: The polling tells a different story than the election fundamentals, though. The 538 polling model gives Democrats an 80 percent chance of losing between two and 30 seats in the House and an 80 percent chance of either losing four seats or gaining two seats in the Senate. Meanwhile, the models over at The Economist give Democrats a five point higher chance of keeping a majority in the House at 23 percent and a two point lower chance of winning a majority in the Senate at 45 percent. This is considerably more optimistic for Democrats than the fundamentals. There are plenty of reasons why outcomes of this election might be less conventional than previous midterms, primarily because voter approval of both parties is low. On one hand, prevailing narratives around things like inflation aren't favorable for President Joe Biden, which trickles down to his party. On the other hand, the GOP has elevated underqualified extreme candidates on the backs of endorsements of Donald Trump, who himself is even more unpopular than President Biden. Most Republican candidates continue to lie about election fraud, and about 70 percent of Republicans polled agree with them. However, over 60 percent of independents polled agree that Biden was legitimately elected, a number that shows just how powerful authoritarianism in the United States has become, by the way. Likewise, only 30 percent of Americans polled approve of the Supreme Court overturning Roe v. Wade, and 74 percent of Democratic or Democratic leaning voters in anti-abortion states polled said that they were more motivated to vote now. However, only 14 percent of voters polled say abortion is top of mind for them when they think about voting in November. Ultimately, with opposite outcomes well within the margin of error in these polling models, it will once again come down to turnout. More than 8 million new voters have aged into eligibility since the last election. These voters are significantly more diverse than the electorate, and they approve of President Biden at a much higher rate than the electorate. But it's harder to turn out first time voters because they haven't done it before. And the youth vote doesn't have even geographic distribution. Also, Republicans have been making gains among parts of the demographic core of the Democratic Party, including Hispanic voters and black male voters. So turnout is anything but predictable.

_transcript: Here's a great question. How do they figure the margin of error in a survey? So, for example, you have a presidential preference survey and you say, if the election were held today, would you vote for candidate A or candidate B? And A has 48% and B has 43%. Then you see a margin of error number, usually somewhere in the neighborhood of 3 to 5%. In surveys, that margin of error is to a 95% confidence interval, which means, say, there's a 3% margin of error. At the 48% number for the candidate A, there is a 95% chance that the actual preference for that candidate among everybody in the country is between 45% and 51%, 3% on either side of the 48%. And it's calculated based on the size of the survey, the number of respondents in the survey. The more respondents, the lower the margin of error. Here's where it gets kind of screwy, though. At least in a presidential election, what really matters is state by state. And even with a very large survey, say 2,000 or 3,000 people, the number of people in a given state might be very small. You might only have a handful of people from Wyoming, for example, who responded. So the margin of error of the poll for just the people in Wyoming would be enormous, as to be meaningless. So that margin of error goes up as you get into subcategories, either, say, gender or income or age, and you get a higher and higher margin of error because there are fewer people in the survey who fit into those categories. It gets even more complex and nuanced than that, but just remember, the number of people surveyed and the margin of error are directly related.
